steps.text: Sector 7. 02:14 AM. The rain hasn't stopped in three days.

Not the clean rain that washes things away — the wrong kind. The kind that sticks to neon signs and makes the whole district glow like a bruise that refuses to fade. The gutters run phosphorescent. The air tastes of ozone and something older, something chemical, something the city stopped apologising for a decade ago.

They say the city never sleeps. That's not true. It just dreams differently — in debt and data, in signal and silence. In the spaces between surveillance nodes where nothing is recorded and everything is remembered by the wrong people.

You are Detective Raines. Fifteen years on the force. Twelve cases that closed too early — not for lack of evidence, but for lack of people willing to see it. You've stopped counting the ones that got buried. You haven't stopped remembering their faces.
Tonight feels different. Tonight the city left a door open. The question — the only question that ever matters at 2 AM in the rain — is whether it did so by mistake.

A body was found in the alley behind the Neon Requiem nightclub. No ID. No witnesses. No prints. No blood. Just a symbol carved into wet asphalt with the precision of someone who had time and a plan — and the silence of a city that has learned, over many long years, to look away.
Raines, you copy? Code Black on Meridian Ave. Homicide needs eyes on the scene NOW. No sirens. No lights. Director's orders.
And Raines — this one's sensitive. Be careful what you log tonight. The Chief has already been briefed. He's watching the channel.
Copy that. Already here. Tell Morrison to keep the uniforms off my perimeter. And tell the Chief that 'sensitive' doesn't make me less curious. It makes me more.
Fifteen years of sensitive cases. You'd think they'd have learned.

The alley behind the Neon Requiem is twelve metres of wet concrete and cold shadow. The club's bass line thumps through the wall — synthetic drums that make it feel like the building itself is breathing. The neon from the rear sign paints the dead man in alternating crimson and blue — a slow strobe that makes it look, for one horrible second at a time, like he might still be breathing.

He is not breathing. The stillness of a dead man is different from sleep. Fifteen years and you never stop noticing the difference. Maybe that's what makes you good at this. Maybe that's what it cost you.

Three things demand your attention simultaneously. The body — always the body first. The perimeter, where the shadows are too deliberate. And the surveillance cameras above the roofline, all three of them angled exactly six degrees away from where you're standing. Not broken. Adjusted.
Forensics arrives in forty minutes. Every second is a decision. Every decision is a direction. In this city the wrong direction doesn't just waste time — it ends investigations.

steps.prompt: How do you begin the investigation?

choices.text: [BODY] Examine the victim. The corpse always speaks first.
[PERIMETER] Sweep the alley. Someone may still be watching this corner.
[TECH] Scout the surveillance angles. This blind spot was engineered.

examine_body.text: Male. Mid-forties. Expensive coat — Italian cut, real wool, the kind a man buys when he's trying to convince someone he belongs somewhere he doesn't. Cheap shoes underneath it. The contradiction of a man caught between two lives.
No visible trauma. No entry wound. No exit wound. No bruising. The body just... stopped. Like a machine powered down from a remote terminal by someone who knew exactly which switch to flip.

The absence of blood is the loudest thing in the alley. Three days of rain and not a trace of biological evidence. This isn't a murder scene — it's a stage set. Someone arranged this with the care of a production designer working to a very specific brief.
Neural link port behind the left ear. Military-grade housing. Civilian-illegal. Whatever this man did for a living, it wasn't anything the licensing board would have approved.
The port is warm. Warmer than the body. Someone accessed this link within the last two hours.

Left breast pocket. A data chip. Small. Smooth. And warm — warmer than the body around it. Someone touched this chip after this man was already dead. Someone who was here first, and left it deliberately.

And carved into the asphalt beneath him — a seven-pointed symbol. Asymmetric at first glance, perfectly precise on second. Not made in haste. Made by someone who had all the time in the world and used every second of it.

Three leads. The neural link — accessed recently by someone who knew how. The chip — left deliberately, still warm. The symbol — a signature placed with care. In this city everything is a message. The question is always: who's the intended reader?

examine_body.prompt: The neural link or the data chip — both accessed after death. Where do you start?

choices.text: [NEURAL LINK] Analyze the neural link. Military tech leaves a deep access log.
[POCKETS] Search the physical pockets thoroughly. The chip isn't alone.

analyze_neural_link.text: Neural link diagnostics. The port housing tells me it was accessed via a military-grade reader — the kind that bypasses consent protocols and pulls the entire short-term memory buffer. Whatever he saw in the last six hours of his life, someone extracted it.
But extractions leave echoes. Ghost traces in the buffer's dead sectors. The deleted data is gone. Its shape is not.
Shape of a face — partial, male, fifties, institutional haircut. Shape of a building interior — glass, steel, corporate. And three letters burned into the data ghost like a brand. M. E. R. Meridian.

Meridian Systems. The largest defense contractor in the sector. The company that runs forty percent of the city's surveillance grid. Whose name appears in eleven sealed federal case files. Whose legal team has won every injunction filed against them in seven years.

He was at Meridian recently. Or Meridian came to him. The distinction matters. One is a meeting. The other is an operation. And the link's final register holds two words burned into the hardware itself: VALE. COVENANT.

analyze_neural_link.prompt: VALE. COVENANT. Two words from a dead man's memory. The station is the next move.

choices.text: [IDENTIFY VALE] Cross-reference the name before going to the station.
[STATION] Go immediately. The Chief was briefed before you were called.

identify_vale_early.text: VALE. Cross-reference: Meridian Systems personnel directory — the unofficial indexed copy that a sloppy archivist posted to an unsecured node three years ago and no one ever scrubbed. The kind of mistake that lives forever in a city built on data.
VALE, MARA. Dr. Senior Cryptographer. Six years at Meridian. Specialisation: data erasure and reconstruction protocols. Current status: sabbatical. As of exactly six weeks ago.
Six weeks. The same window when three separate cold cases were re-flagged internally and then buried again within forty-eight hours each. Not a coincidence. A trigger event.

A cryptographer on sabbatical whose name appears in the ghost-trace of a dead man's neural buffer. A woman who knows how to make data disappear — who may have made herself disappear for the same reasons. The station is the next move. The Chief was briefed early, and that sequence of information is the whole shape of the trap.

identify_vale_early.prompt: Vale is in the wind. The Chief is at the station. Where first?

choices.text: [STATION] Report in. Find out what the Chief already knows.
[SYMBOL] The carving in the asphalt — photograph it before leaving the scene.

search_physical_pockets.text: Data chip in the breast pocket. But a thorough search means thorough — right through to the lining. People who carry important things often hide more important things behind them.
Inner lining. Stitched pocket — hand-sewn, not factory. A recent modification. Someone altered this coat specifically to carry something in a place a standard pat-down wouldn't find.

A folded card. Printed, not digital. Real paper — the paranoid redundancy of a man who's spent enough years around people who read data remotely. On the card: eight case file numbers. Seven are crossed out in red ink. The eighth is circled.
The circled number is mine. Case ID: Raines, J. Active Investigator. Cross-referenced to tonight's callout.

He wasn't just left here. He was left here for you. Specifically. He knew you'd be called to this scene — which means someone told him how case assignments work in Special Investigations. That list is not public information. Assignment records are controlled by one office.

A kill list with your name uncrossed. Seven dead. One remaining. A dead man who arranged his own corpse as a message. In fifteen years you have never seen anything quite like this — and that means you're dealing with someone who has been at this considerably longer than you have.

search_physical_pockets.prompt: He died to leave you this message. The Chief is at the station. What first?

choices.text: [STATION] Go immediately. The Chief knows something.
[CHIP] Pocket the chip and find a ghost reader before anyone else gets to it.

examine_symbol_early.text: Seven points. Each equidistant to within a millimetre. This wasn't made freehand in the rain at 2 AM. Someone brought a template. Someone prepared this the way you prepare a signature — practiced, precise, completely intentional.
I've seen variations of this symbol in three separate case files. All closed. All ruled misadventure or natural causes. All assigned to investigators who no longer work in this department.

A signature is a claim of authorship. You sign your name on things you're proud of — or on things you want someone specific to know you're capable of. This symbol was not left for the police. It was left for whoever was going to be sent to this scene.

examine_symbol_early.prompt: The symbol connects to sealed files. The Chief is at the station.

choices.text: [STATION] Go to the station. The Chief knows more than he sent.

secure_perimeter.text: Secondary exit. Roof access. A ladder that's been oiled within the last twenty-four hours. Building maintenance doesn't operate at 2 AM unless someone arranged for it specifically. The kind of arrangement that doesn't appear on any schedule.

There's a sound behind the dumpster. Not a rat. Something heavier, breathing very carefully. I've learned the difference between the silence of an empty alley and the silence of someone trying very hard to be part of one.
Please — please don't. I'm not involved. I sleep here. I've slept here for two months. I didn't see anything.
Nobody says they didn't see anything before they're asked what they saw. What's your name?

Fear is a useful diagnostic. Everyone is afraid of something specific, and the nature of that specific fear is information. This person is afraid of being identified — not of the police. That distinction tells you something important about how they came to be here.

secure_perimeter.prompt: A witness who says they saw nothing. How do you get the truth?

choices.text: [PRESSURE] Make the cost of silence very clear. Fast and direct.
[EMPATHY] Step back. Give them a reason to trust you over their fear.
[TRADE] Offer invisibility — no record, no name. Information for safety.

witness_pressure.text: Here's your situation. You are twenty metres from a homicide. You have no alibi. Your presence here is already logged by dispatch. In thirty minutes forensics arrives and you become their first question. I'm the better option — talk to me now.

A car. Black, no plates. North end of the alley, engine running for forty minutes. Two people got out. The dead man was already here waiting — he looked scared but like someone who had decided to be scared and keep going anyway.
One of them talked to him. The other went up the ladder. I heard what the talker said just before the dead man fell. Word for word.

'You remembered too much. The Covenant settles its debts.' Then nothing. No shot. No struggle. He just sat down against the wall. And the man from the car walked back and got in. Calm. Like he'd just finished a meeting.

The Covenant. The word lands like something dropped from a great height. You've heard it in three sealed case files, each of which closed before you could finish reading it. Each time the word appeared, the file disappeared within seventy-two hours.

Two operators. Coordinated exit. 'You remembered too much.' Memory is the crime. Information is the motive. This is institutional. And the Chief was briefed before I was called — which means this connects somewhere above my pay grade and below my radar.

witness_pressure.prompt: The Covenant. Two operators. A witness with dangerous knowledge. Where next?

choices.text: [STATION] Take this to the station. Face the Chief directly.
[PROTECT] This witness knows too much to leave here alone tonight.

witness_protection_detour.text: The Covenant heard what they needed from a dead man. The last thing this operation needs is a living witness who can describe their vehicle and quote their script. People who can quote operational language don't stay unnoticed long in this city.

Raines places the witness with a safehouse contact — one of three people in the department whose loyalty runs to the job rather than the hierarchy. Then he turns toward the station. The Chief is waiting. The Chief was briefed. The shape of that briefing is the shape of the investigation.

witness_protection_detour.prompt: Witness secured. Now face the Chief.

choices.text: [STATION] Go to the police station. This conversation is overdue.

witness_empathy.text: Hey. I'm stepping back. You're not in trouble. I'm not here to add to whatever you're already carrying tonight. There's a man dead twenty metres from here. Whatever you saw is going to live in you whether you tell me or not. I'm just asking if you want it to mean something.

...He'd been here twice this week. Same corner, same time. Like he was keeping an appointment with himself. Tonight someone came. I didn't see the face. But I heard the words. Word for word, because I was very still and trying to be part of the wall.
'You remembered too much. The Covenant settles its debts.' Then quiet. No violence. No struggle. He just chose the wall and slid down it.

He chose the wall. A man who knew this was coming and came anyway. The only reason to do that is if you're delivering something. Or if you've stopped caring what happens next and started caring about what happens after.

witness_empathy.prompt: He came here deliberately. The Covenant ordered this. The station is next.

choices.text: [STATION] Face the Chief. He was briefed before you were called.
[SYMBOL] Before you leave — photograph the carving. It appears in three sealed files.

witness_trade.text: I can make tonight disappear for you. No record, no report, no mention of your name in any file that exists or ever will. In this city the ability to not exist in a database is worth more than money. I'm offering you invisibility.
Under the third step of the fire escape. He put something there before they came. I watched him do it — like he was leaving a note for someone he trusted would come looking.
Under the third step: a folded card. Printed, not handwritten. A list of eight case file numbers. Seven crossed out in red ink. The eighth circled. The eighth is Raines.

He hid this knowing he might not survive. He came here anyway. That's not fear anymore — that's conviction. The most dangerous thing in this city is a man who has decided that what he knows is worth dying for.

My name on a kill list. Case assignments controlled by one office. Director Crane. The Chief was briefed early. The sequence is wrong in a way that only makes sense if the whole night was choreographed.

witness_trade.prompt: Your name is the last on the list. Go to the station.

choices.text: [STATION] Go now. Find out if the Chief is part of this.

surveillance_sweep.text: Three cameras. All covering this perimeter. All angled exactly six degrees away from the crime scene. Not damaged — adjusted. The kind of adjustment that requires physical access to the junction boxes and a knowledge of the surveillance grid detailed enough to know exactly how far to move them.

This blind spot was engineered. It was in the plans before the body arrived. Someone spent real time on this — professional time. The junction box seal is broken. Recent — the edge still clean, no oxidisation. Someone was inside it tonight, within the last three hours.

Four seconds of recovered footage before the wipe protocol re-activates. A figure in profile. A Meridian Systems ID badge — black lanyard, silver housing. A partial vehicle plate at the north end: V and R.

VR. VALE RESEARCH. A shell company name. A Meridian badge. A redirected surveillance grid. The company that runs forty percent of our surveillance was here tonight, working against it. That is not a coincidence. That is an operation.

The station is the next move. The Chief was briefed before the call came to you. Information moves fastest to the people who most need to control it. Understanding what Morales knows — and what he's been told to say — is the foundation of everything that follows.

surveillance_sweep.prompt: A Meridian badge at a Meridian-engineered blind spot. Take it to the station.

choices.text: [STATION] Go to the station. The Chief is the next piece.
[BADGE] Cross-reference the badge number before showing your hand to anyone.

badge_crossref_early.text: Unofficial Meridian employee registry. An archivist's mistake that lives forever on an unsecured node — the kind of immortal error that a city built on data generates constantly and never truly purges.

VALE, MARA. Senior Cryptographer. Clearance: black level. Status: sabbatical. But this badge was active tonight. At 01:47 AM. In that alley. A woman on sabbatical whose access credentials were used at a murder scene sixteen minutes before the murder was reported.

Three possibilities. She ordered it. She witnessed it. Or someone stole her credentials specifically to frame her if anyone started looking. A cryptographer who specialises in data erasure. Whose sabbatical coincides with an acceleration in someone's operational tempo. This is not coincidence.

badge_crossref_early.prompt: Vale's badge was here. She's hiding or running. The station is next.

choices.text: [STATION] Go to the station. Chief Morales must be confronted.

yevgeny_first.text: Tier 4. The laundry exists in a gap between two condemned buildings that the city decided were too expensive to demolish and too dangerous to inhabit. The gap is just wide enough for a door, a counter, and whatever business Yevgeny conducts behind the curtain of dry-cleaning bags that fills the back third of the space.

The smell is perchloroethylene and burnt solder and the particular staleness of a room where someone has been afraid for a very long time. Yevgeny's business model depends on being the kind of man that frightened people trust. He has perfected the aesthetics of that role.
Raines. You look like the rain got inside you. Sit down before you fall.
No time. The chip. Military-grade housing. Covenant encryption if I'm reading the shell correctly. I need to know what's on it before someone wipes it remotely.

Covenant. You said Covenant, Raines. I need you to understand something. There are three jobs I have refused in eleven years of this work. All three were Covenant jobs. I am still alive because I refused them.
My name is on their list. Eighth slot. The others are already crossed out. Read the chip or I mention your basement operation to my less forgiving colleagues.

Yevgeny works for nine minutes in absolute silence. His hands are precise and completely still. His face is not. He has the expression of a man who has accidentally walked into a room where something is happening that he will spend years trying to forget.
Coordinates — redacted. Eight case file numbers, seven flagged complete, one active. And a name. VALE. Not a person — a handler designation. A codename for whoever sits at the top of this structure.

But below the handler data — something else. A real name. Dr. Mara Vale. Meridian Systems. She built the encryption on this chip. She also left a back door in it. Deliberately. This chip was designed to be found by someone who knew how to look.

She's not the handler. She's the whistleblower. The Covenant used her name as a designation — if anyone traced it, they'd find her instead of themselves. She's been set up as the fall. And she knew it. And she built a door out anyway.

The station. The Chief is there. He was briefed before you were called. The sequence of that information matters more than anything Yevgeny just told you. Understanding what Morales knows — and what he was told to contain — is the shape of the trap you may already be inside.

yevgeny_first.prompt: Vale built the back door. The Chief was briefed early. Face Morales now.

choices.text: [STATION] Go to the station. Confront the Chief about what he knows.
[GHOST] Find Ghost — the underground hacker network can locate Vale faster.

ghost_contact_early.text: Cyber Alley. A narrow corridor between two server farm annexes whose heat exhaust turns the passage into something between a sauna and a server room. The concrete walls pulse with residual electromagnetic field. Ghost operates from somewhere in this corridor — the specific somewhere shifts every forty-eight hours.
Detective Raines. You've never come to me directly before. Something changed tonight.
I need a location. Dr. Mara Vale. Former Meridian cryptographer, six weeks off-grid. Whatever underground network is hiding her, find the node.

Ghost works in silence that has texture — the sound of systems being accessed, of firewalls being navigated with the particular grace of someone who has spent years treating information architecture the way a musician treats an instrument. Eleven minutes of that productive silence.

Vale is alive. Three weeks at a location the underground maintains for people who need to stop existing for a while. She's been waiting — she built a back door into Covenant encryption specifically to be found by the right person at the right moment.
But she won't come to you. And before you go to her — the Chief is already monitoring Vale's name in departmental searches. Morales knows she's a thread. He's watching to see who pulls it first.
Then the station has to be first. I need to understand what Morales is protecting before I give him a reason to move against me.

ghost_contact_early.prompt: The Chief is watching Vale's name. Go to the station first.

choices.text: [STATION] Station. Chief Morales. Find out what he's protecting.

police_station_arrival.text: The Sector 7 station. 03:22 AM. The building smells of recycled air, bad coffee, and the particular institutional fatigue of a place that processes human tragedy on a shift rotation. The fluorescent lights hum at a frequency designed, apparently, to make everyone inside slightly more miserable than they would otherwise be.

The night-shift officers move with the careful economy of people who have learned to save their energy for the moments that actually require it. They nod at Raines. They don't ask questions. In Special Investigations, not asking questions is a professional skill — and tonight, a survival instinct.

Chief Morales' office is at the end of the corridor. The light is on. At 03:22 AM the light in the Chief's office being on means one of three things: he's working, he's waiting, or he already knows you're here. In this case, Raines suspects all three.
I'll stand. The body on Meridian Ave — you were briefed before I received the call. I'd like to understand the sequence of that information.
There are aspects of this case that operate above your clearance level, Detective. I need you to understand that before this conversation goes any further.
Everything in this city operates above my clearance level. That has never once stopped me from looking at it.

Morales stands. Moves to the window. The rain outside has intensified — sheets of it now, the neon of the street below bleeding upward against the glass like something trying to get inside. He keeps his back to Raines for exactly long enough to be a deliberate statement.

There is pressure from above, Raines. Significant pressure. People with institutional weight are watching this case before the case file even exists. That tells you something about the nature of that pressure.
I am telling you to be careful. I am not telling you to stop. There is a difference — and the fact that I'm making it right now is the only thing I can give you tonight.

Morales doesn't answer. The not-answering is its own kind of answer. In fifteen years Raines has learned to read the grammar of institutional silence — the specific silence of a man who knows he can neither confirm nor deny without consequences he hasn't fully calculated yet.
I have a witness in holding. Picked up two blocks from the scene ninety minutes before the body was found. She's been asking for a detective by name. Your name, Raines.
The fact that she knows your name before you're on the case means someone planned for you to be on this case. I need you to understand what that implies about your safety tonight.

A witness asking for Raines by name. Picked up before the murder was officially reported. The sequence is wrong in a way that only makes sense if the whole night was choreographed — every piece placed in advance by someone who understood exactly how the city's response system would move.

police_station_arrival.prompt: A witness asking for you by name. How do you approach this?

choices.text: [INTERROGATION ROOM] Go in direct. She knows your name — she planned for this.
[CHIEF FIRST] Press Morales harder. His knowledge is the foundation of the trap.

press_the_chief.text: Before I go in there — I need to know what you know about Director Crane's involvement in active Covenant operations. A witness who knows my name before I'm assigned got that name from someone with access to assignment records. That's one office.

I know that certain cases in this department have been closed by influence that doesn't appear in any paperwork I've signed. I know that the Covenant's name appears in sealed federal files I've been told never to access. I know Crane has connections to Meridian Systems that are not disclosed in any ethics filing.

What I don't know — what I've been very carefully prevented from knowing — is the operational detail. That detail is in the room down the hall. With a woman who asked for you specifically. Go find out why.
One more question. Are you going to report this conversation to Crane?
I'm going to get another coffee. My memory of the last twenty minutes is going to be adversely affected by exhaustion and poor institutional lighting. That's the best I can offer you, Raines.

Morales bought you a window. He knows more than he's saying and less than he needs to. He's protecting himself from a position with no safe exits — the position every honest official eventually reaches inside a corrupt system. Use the window while it's open.

press_the_chief.prompt: Morales gave you a window. The witness is down the hall.

choices.text: [INTERROGATION ROOM] Go in now. She asked for you. Find out why.

interrogation_room_entry.text: Interrogation Room Three. The smallest one — the one they use when they want the space itself to apply pressure. Four metres by four metres of grey wall, a table with a ring anchor, two chairs, and a mirror that everyone in the room understands perfectly well is not a mirror.

The woman across the table doesn't look like someone who needs managing. She looks like someone who has been managing herself very carefully for a very long time and has only now chosen to stop. Late thirties. Sharp eyes doing continuous threat assessment since Raines walked through the door. Hands flat on the table — visible, deliberate, the body language of someone who knows exactly how they appear and has made a specific choice about it.
Detective Raines. You look exactly like your case file photograph. That's unusual — most people look worse in person.
You know my name. You asked for me before I was assigned to a case that didn't officially exist ninety minutes ago. Who are you, and why are you here?
My name is Lena Sorel. I worked for Meridian Systems for four years as a junior data analyst. Eighteen months ago I discovered something in the erasure logs that I wasn't supposed to discover.

A pattern. Eight names cycled through the erasure queue over three years. Six were historical — cold cases already closed. Two were flagged as upcoming. One of those two was the man you found tonight.
The other upcoming name on the erasure queue is yours, Detective. It's been there for eleven months.

The room is very small. The fluorescent light hums in the specific frequency of institutional displacement — the sound of a system designed to make you feel like a variable in an equation rather than a person asking a question.

Eleven months. Your name has been in their system for eleven months. Every case you've worked in that time, every file you've accessed, every lead you've followed — all of it watched by people who were deciding when, not whether.

interrogation_room_entry.prompt: She's been watching your case file for eleven months. How do you proceed?

choices.text: [TRUST HER] She came here voluntarily and asked for you. That's not a cover story.
[PRESS HER] She knows too much. Either she's genuine or she's the most sophisticated plant you've met.
[TEST HER] Ask something only a real Meridian insider would know. Verify before trusting.

interrogation_trust.text: You came here. You asked for me by name. You're telling me things that put you in danger simply by virtue of your knowing them. That's not a cover story. Cover stories don't volunteer liability. Tell me everything about the erasure queue — and tell me about Dr. Mara Vale.

The queue is maintained by the Covenant through a Meridian back-end system that Dr. Vale built — Project CHRONOS. She didn't build it for this purpose. She built it as a legitimate data management tool. They repurposed it.

When Vale discovered what her tool was being used for, she ran. But before she left, she built a back door into the encryption. A way for someone to read the Covenant's own operational records using the same key they use to hide them.

She gave the back door's location to the man you found tonight. He was supposed to pass it to you in person. They got to him before the handoff. But the back door still exists. And I know where to access it.

He died delivering a back door he never got to hand over. Vale is still out there with the full picture. And this woman knows the access point. Three separate pieces of the same puzzle appearing on the same night — either extraordinary luck or a setup several layers deeper than anything I've seen before.
I'm choosing to believe it's luck. Because the alternative means someone is smarter than I am, and I can't afford that possibility right now.

interrogation_trust.prompt: Sorel knows where the back door is. How do you proceed?

choices.text: [NIGHT CLUB] The access point is at the Neon Requiem. Go there now.
[VALE FIRST] Find Vale before accessing the back door. You need the full picture.

interrogation_press.text: Let's talk about the timeline. You knew a murder was going to happen tonight at that specific location. You were picked up two blocks away ninety minutes before it was reported. The mathematics of that sequence are very inconvenient for your story.
I knew because I've been tracking the Covenant's operational schedule for three months. I knew tonight was the handoff attempt. I came to observe — to have a witness unconnected to either side.
You knew about an active operation and didn't report it. That makes you either complicit or foolish. Which one are you?

I didn't report it because the last two people who reported Covenant activity to this department disappeared from case files within a week. I came to you specifically because your file shows twelve cases that closed too early — and a reputation for not letting cases close before they're finished.

She knows about the twelve cases. That is not in my public file. That is in the internal performance review that only three people in this department can access. Either she has a source inside — or she is the source.

The pressure worked — not to break her, but to surface something she was about to withhold. The detail about the twelve cases is the kind that only surfaces under pressure. It's also the kind only a genuine insider would know.

interrogation_press.prompt: She knows your internal file. She's either very well connected or exactly who she says she is.

choices.text: [NIGHT CLUB] She says the access point is at the Neon Requiem. Go there.
[KEEP PRESSING] One more round. Find what she's still holding back.

interrogation_final_press.text: You know twelve cases from my internal review. That review was accessed three times in the last six weeks by someone using administrative credentials. Was that you?

...Yes. I needed to understand whether you were the right person. Whether you were still looking for the thing they'd taken away from you twelve times. Whether the system had finished you or just slowed you down.
The answer, in case you were wondering, was clearly not finished. Which is why I'm in this room instead of anywhere safer.

She chose him. Selected him from available options the way you select a tool for a specific job — by understanding what the job requires and which tool has survived similar work before. In this city that is either very flattering or very calculated. The two are rarely mutually exclusive.

interrogation_final_press.prompt: She chose you deliberately. Trust the selection and move.

choices.text: [NIGHT CLUB] The access point. The Neon Requiem. Go now.

interrogation_test.text: Before this conversation goes further — what's the internal Meridian designation for the data management system Dr. Vale built? The one in their internal architecture docs under a codename that's never been made public.

CHRONOS. The Meridian internal name is Project CHRONOS. Its function is the management of time — specifically, the removal of events from the recorded timeline. Vale named it herself, before she understood what they'd use it for.

CHRONOS. The name that appears in the one Meridian document I accessed before the sealed file closed in my face. The name that no one outside Meridian's top-level architecture team would have. She's real. She knows it because she was there.

The test passed. She's a genuine Meridian insider who saw something in the architecture of their own system that couldn't be unseen — and chose this specific night and this specific detective as the point where the information moved from hiding to action.

night_club_scene.text: The Neon Requiem. From the outside, an alley and a body. From the inside — four floors of synthetic fog, bass frequencies designed to bypass rational thought, and the particular social ecology of a city that processes its fear through choreographed abandon.

The main floor pulses with bodies and sound. The neon is everywhere — violet and cyan and deep amber, overlapping in the fog until the whole space looks like the inside of a data transmission, like being inside the city's dreams rather than walking through its streets.

The server room is on sub-level one. Every club of this type has one — the network infrastructure that keeps the payment systems, the membership records, and the security feeds operational. The kind of room that looks mundane and is anything but. Raines moves through the crowd without his badge. Tonight, arrival should be quiet.

According to Sorel, Vale's back door into Project CHRONOS is accessible from any node that connects to the Meridian sub-grid. The Neon Requiem runs on Meridian infrastructure. This whole district does. That was the point — hide the access point in plain sight, in a place too busy and too loud for anyone to notice a quiet data query at 4 AM.

Sub-level one. The server room. The bass from the floor above vibrates through the racks of equipment and turns the entire space into something between a data centre and a percussion instrument. The access terminal is at the far end. Blinking. Waiting.
You're Ghost. You're in the Neon Requiem server room at 04:00 AM. Either you anticipated this or you were already here.

Ghost works with the particular grace of someone who treats information systems the way a musician treats an instrument — not a tool to be operated but a collaborator to be understood. The terminal responds to their touch differently than it would to anyone else's. The data begins to move.

The back door is open. Vale built it beautifully — seven years of Covenant operational records accessible through a read-only port that their own security can't see because Vale designed their security. This is the most elegant act of revenge I've ever seen executed in code.

Accessing it triggers a passive alarm. Not immediate — delayed. We have approximately forty minutes before Covenant security receives notification that someone is reading what they've been hiding. Choose what you want most.
In forty minutes I want Director Crane's operational logs. The identity of whoever the Covenant designates as the Architect. And the full authorisation chain for the kill order with my name on it.

Ghost works. The data moves through the back door in careful streams — each record a thread in a seven-year pattern of institutional crime. Cases closed. Witnesses silenced. Information erased at the precise moment it became dangerous. The methodology of a system that has learned to protect itself by consuming the tools meant to expose it.

And there, in the Covenant's own operational logs, under an access handle appearing in sixty-seven separate authorisation records across seven years: ARCHITECT. And a real name beneath it. One that reorganises everything Raines thought he understood about who is protected in this city and why.

Raines. The Architect is Senator Calloway. Federal oversight committee. The man whose committee is responsible for reviewing exactly this kind of criminal organisation. He built the Covenant from inside the mechanism designed to stop it.

A senator. Not a criminal who hid inside the system. A legislator who built the oversight mechanism specifically to control what it was supposed to prevent. Seven years. Sixty-seven authorisations. Eight names on a list. That's not corruption. That's architecture.

Thirty-two minutes remain before the passive alarm reaches Covenant security. The data is downloaded. The evidence exists. The question is what to do with it. In this city, evidence is only as powerful as the channel through which it moves. The wrong channel makes it disappear. The right channel makes it unstoppable.

[VALE] Find Dr. Vale first. Her testimony plus this data is truly unstoppable.
[CHIEF] Take this to Morales. He protected you tonight — maybe he can protect this too.

underground_search_ch2.text: Below the grid. The underground network that runs beneath official infrastructure like a second nervous system — slower, quieter, and infinitely more honest about what it is and what it does.
Old relay station at the Meridian Grid boundary. Grid reference seven. She'll be there until dawn. After that she moves — different location, different protocol, considerably harder to find.

The Covenant has been searching for six weeks. Tonight's operation was designed partly to flush her out — if the dead man had successfully made contact with you, Vale would have known the handoff was complete and moved to the next phase. Instead she's still waiting. And the Covenant is still looking.

The relay station. The rain is heavier now — the kind that makes the city look like it's dissolving at the edges, all neon and concrete and running water blurring into a single wet light. Raines moves through it with the particular focus of someone who has stopped thinking about whether and is only thinking about how.
Detective Raines. You made it. They told me the handoff was compromised. I've been waiting to find out if you'd come anyway.
Dr. Vale. What's on the drives?

Seven years of Covenant records. Every operational order. Every authorised deletion. Every name — including the Architect. Including the people above Crane who gave him his instructions and the federal protections that made those instructions possible.
I built the system they used. I also built the way to undo it. I've been waiting for someone with enough left to still care about the difference between what's recorded and what's true.

A sound from the north entrance. Multiple operators — the Covenant found the relay station, whether through surveillance or a leak in the underground network. Three operatives moving toward the building with the efficiency of people who have done this before and fully intend to do it cleanly.

[FIGHT] Three operators. Find a way through.

ch2_broadcast_ending.text: The broadcast goes out on eleven independent receivers simultaneously. Not a single centralised channel that can be killed with one call to one office — eleven separate nodes, each in a different jurisdiction, each archived the moment the signal arrives.

Three investigative journalists. Four federal oversight analysts not on Senator Calloway's committee. Two independent archive nodes maintained by organisations that have been waiting for exactly this kind of material for years. Two international legal bodies whose jurisdiction extends beyond the reach of anything the Covenant can touch.

Seven years of records. Sixty-seven operational authorisations. Eight kills — seven completed, one that didn't land — and the full structural map of a criminal organisation that used the oversight mechanism designed to stop it as its primary protection.
Senator Calloway's name appears four hundred and twelve times in the operational logs. That's not a framing. That's a career built on other people's endings.

Director Crane is detained before dawn. Senator Calloway resigns his committee position at 06:00 AM — three hours before the warrant is issued, which tells you everything about how well-connected his legal team is and how little that matters when the evidence is in twelve jurisdictions simultaneously.

Dr. Mara Vale testifies for eighteen hours over three days. Her testimony is the key that opens every lock the Covenant built over seven years. She built those locks. She knows where every single one of them is — and she built each one with a second door that only she knew about.
Raines. You're suspended pending departmental review. You know that.
Three months. Maybe two if the oversight board moves quickly. Which it will, given the circumstances.
Seven cases reopened. Three months of suspension. I've had worse ratios.

Raines walks out of the station at 06:47 AM. The rain has stopped. For the first time in three days, the city exists without that constant wet weight — the pavement steams slightly where the neon signs have been running hot all night, and the light has that particular early-morning quality of a world that has not yet decided whether the previous night was a dream or a decision.
Seven families receive phone calls that morning. Seven cases, reopened. Seven answers to questions that have been waiting for years in the specific silence of unresolved grief.

In the city's data grid, in eleven independent archives, in the legal filings of two international bodies, in the testimony record of a cryptographer who built a back door into the system that wanted to erase her — the truth exists now. In multiple copies. In multiple jurisdictions. In places too numerous and too distributed to close.
Fifteen years. Twelve cases closed too early. One that finally wasn't.

That's the thing about truth in a city built on data. It's not that it can't be deleted. It's that deleting it everywhere simultaneously is harder than building it was in the first place. And building it took one detective, one night, and a dead man who decided that what he knew was worth the cost of delivering it.
>> CHAPTER II ENDING ACHIEVED: THE ARCHITECT FALLS — The Covenant is dismantled. The city breathes differently. The case is closed — and this time, it stays that way.

ch2_chief_ending.text: Raines. You look like you've been through something significant.

Seven years of Covenant operational records. Senator Calloway as the Architect. Director Crane as operational lead. Sixty-seven authorised eliminations, eight of which we can directly prosecute. I need a channel that doesn't route through anyone Crane can reach in the next six hours.

Morales reads. For a very long time. In the silence of a man absorbing information that reorganises everything he thought he understood about the institution he's spent his career inside — every closed case, every sealed file, every conversation that ended too quickly now reframed in the light of what Raines has placed on his desk.

There is a federal prosecutor in District Three who has been building a Covenant-adjacent case for two years without knowing what connects the structure to the authorising authority. She's been working without the evidence that names the architect.

I'm going to make a call. And Raines — when the review board asks what I knew and when I knew it, I'm going to tell them I acted on a detective's evidence the moment it was presented to me. That's the story. Make sure it's accurate.

The call takes four minutes. The federal case absorbs the Covenant evidence within the hour. Director Crane is detained before his morning briefing. Senator Calloway's office issues a statement about an 'ongoing personal matter' at exactly the moment the warrant is signed — the legal team's instinct for self-preservation is impeccable, and in this case, completely insufficient.

The case is filed. The evidence is in federal custody, in a jurisdiction and with a prosecutor who cannot be touched by the system that was protecting it. Seven families receive answers across three careful days.

Morales made the right call when it counted. In this city that's worth noting. Most people wait for the right call to be the safe call — they're usually the same call, eventually. Tonight they were different, and he chose the right one anyway.
>> CHAPTER II ENDING ACHIEVED: THROUGH PROPER CHANNELS — The truth found its way through a system designed to stop it. Sometimes that's the most remarkable ending of all.

ch2_cornered_ending.text: Three operators. A relay station with two exits, both covered. Vale behind me with seven years of evidence. If the evidence goes out before they reach us, the operation ends regardless of what happens to us. I need forty seconds.
I can give you forty seconds. The broadcast is already initialised. I just need to confirm the eleven receivers and initiate the transfer. Go.

Forty seconds. One doorway. Three operators who are very good at their work. Raines is also very good at his — just at a different kind of work, in a different kind of language. The language of people who stay standing when the system wants them to fall.

The broadcast goes out at second thirty-seven. The operators reach the server room at second forty-two. The evidence is already in eleven places at once. The five seconds between those two moments is the entire history of this investigation, compressed into the only outcome that mattered.

Raines is detained. Vale is taken into what the operators call 'protective custody' — a phrase that means something very different depending on who's using it. But the evidence is out. In places they cannot reach.
They detain the messenger. The message is already everywhere. In this city — in any city — that's the only victory that actually holds.

Director Crane is arrested forty-eight hours later when the first federal warrant lands. Senator Calloway's legal team fights for three weeks and then stops fighting, which is its own kind of confession.

Raines is released without charges. The evidence he gathered was collected in ways that are legally complicated but ultimately correct — the kind of correct that the law recognises when it has no other choice.
>> CHAPTER II ENDING ACHIEVED: THE MESSAGE SURVIVES — The cost was significant. The result was permanent. In this city, that's a better ratio than most.

ch2_escape_ending.text: Raines knows this building. He knew it before he entered it — because the first rule of any operation in a city you know well is to understand the exits before you need them. The second rule is to remember that the exits people plan are never the exits that save you.
The maintenance shaft. Sub-level access to the storm drainage system. It connects to the old Meridian service tunnels — infrastructure they decommissioned five years ago and forgot to secure.
They built a city on data and forgot to secure the physical infrastructure. The analog gap in a digital system. The crack that everything important moves through, eventually.

The maintenance shaft. The storm tunnels. The old Meridian service infrastructure that runs beneath the city like the skeleton of an earlier version of itself. Rain water moves through it. Evidence moves through it. Raines and Vale move through it, carrying seven years of files in a waterproof case that Vale has been maintaining for exactly this contingency.

She prepared for this escape. She prepared for many escapes. A cryptographer's mind builds redundancy into everything — because the thing that fails is always the thing you were most certain wouldn't.

Crane seals the department file. Lists the investigation as inactive. Officially, nothing happened tonight. Officially, the body on Meridian Ave is an open case that will never quite close. Officially, I'm on administrative leave for conduct unbecoming.

But we're alive. The evidence is across three off-grid locations. And Vale is somewhere in the city with the key to everything the Covenant spent seven years building — and the seven years she spent learning how to take it apart.

I've been a detective for fifteen years. I've learned how to wait. I've learned how to hold a truth until the city is ready to hear it. This truth is ready. It just needs the right moment — and in this city, the right moments always come, because the wrong ones accumulate until the weight becomes impossible to ignore.

The rain stops at 05:53 AM. For the first time in three days, the city exists without that constant wet weight. The pavement steams. The neon signs run in the clean air. Somewhere beneath the city, in tunnels that are supposed to be empty, a detective and a cryptographer plan the next move.
The truth exists. In multiple copies. In three locations. Waiting — with the particular patience of something that doesn't need to rush because it's already happened and cannot be made to unhappen.
>> CHAPTER II ENDING ACHIEVED: BENEATH THE CITY — The case is not closed. But the truth is preserved, and the investigation continues below the grid. Chapter Three begins in the dark.
